sn_lead: Using the Shinooka Village History (1927), this page traces how the name “Shinooka” came about.
sn_p1: It began in 1144, when fields in Shinogi district were recognized as an estate. The Shinogi estate spanned today’s Komaki and Kasugai. A list of villages based on the Edo-period gazetteer Choshu Fushi (張州府志) names Noguchi, Oyama and Okusa along with Kozoji, Jinryo and Utsutsu.
sn_p2: The Ajioka estate lay in today’s Komaki, and its name appears in a record from 1101. An Edo-period gazetteer cited in the Komaki City History lists 15 villages, including Komaki, Iwasaki, Komatsuji and Honjo. According to the village history, Shinooka bordered Shinogi Village to the south and Ajioka Village to the west. Its extent is only estimated, from today’s Ajioka and Honjo in Komaki through the city center to Dengaku in northern Kasugai.
sn_q_h: Original text (excerpt from Chapter 1, Section 1 of the village history)
sn_q_n: Copied as printed, including old character forms and spellings such as 鷹木村.
sn_s1_h: What the Village History Says<small>村誌に書かれた由来</small>
sn_s1_p: According to the village history, seven eastern settlements were divided between two estates in medieval times. In reference to this, the village was called Shinooka from the 1906 merger. The characters read as the “Shino” of Shinogi joined to the “oka” of Ajioka, but the history does not say outright that one character was taken from each.
sn_s2_h: How Far the Two Estates Reached<small>二つの荘園の広がり</small>
sn_s3_h: This Site’s View<small>当サイトの見解</small>
sn_s3_n: How the name Tokadai was chosen has not been confirmed, so we cannot say it was meant as a compromise.
sn_s3_p: 🔎 This site’s hypothesis: “Shinooka” can be seen as a compromise name that drew on both estates and favored neither. “Tokadai” may have been a more developed form of that compromise, since it uses none of the existing settlement names and is taken instead from a view everyone shared: the peach orchards on the eastern hills.
sn_src: Sources: Shinooka Village History (篠岡村誌), Shinooka Village History Editorial Office, 1927, opening of Chapter 1. The extent of the estates follows a personal local-history website, “Notes on Medieval Estates around Komaki and Kasugai” (Japanese), which cites the Kasugai and Komaki city histories and Choshu Fushi. We have not yet checked the city histories themselves. The founding year and the estimated extent of the Ajioka estate follow the Kasugai and Komaki pages of Local Historia.
sn_warn: The sources differ on one point. The Kasugai and Komaki city histories both call the extent of the Ajioka estate “unknown.” Hayashi, Ikenouchi, Kamisue and Shimosue are not among the 15 villages above, and Choshu Fushi and other works list these four under the Kumano (Rokushi) estate. The village history is best read as showing how local people understood the matter in the early Showa era.
